theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Labour on a job costs J$24 000 and materials J$36 000. The contractor adds 20% to the total cost. What is the price before GCT, in J$?
What name is given to the customers who owe the business money for work already invoiced?
A van costing J$3 600 000 should last 6 years and be worth nothing at the end. Using straight-line depreciation, what is the depreciation each year, in J$?
What is the name of the profit left after all costs, including overheads, are taken away from income?
What is the name of the profit worked out as sales minus only the direct costs of the jobs?
What do the letters NIS stand for, in the payroll deductions made in Jamaica?
What is the name of the priced offer a contractor sends in competition with other firms to win a large job from a builder or a public body?
What do we call the small share of the contract price that the client holds back until any defects in the work are put right?
A firm's fixed costs are J$240 000 a month. Each job leaves J$20 000 towards them after its own costs. How many jobs a month are needed to break even?
What is the name for a small amount of money kept in the office for small purchases, such as a box of wire connectors?
On a J$200 000 solar install, the profit is J$50 000. What percentage of the selling price is profit?
What two-word term means work that comes from past clients returning to the firm again and again?
What kind of insurance covers a firm's own workers if they are injured at work?
What two-word name is given to the money tied up in stock, debtors and cash that keeps a business running from day to day?
What is the name of the statement that lists a business's assets, liabilities and the owner's equity on one date?

essays.stem: Set out a five-year plan for becoming the owner of a small electrical contracting firm, with yearly milestones for licensing, experience, savings, equipment and first clients. Explain why each milestone matters.
essays.modelAnswer: In year one I would keep my job, finish my Level 3, and gain the licence the law requires to certify installations, because without it I cannot legally sign off my own work. I would start saving a set amount each month. In year two I would widen my experience, for example in solar PV and generator changeovers, and learn pricing and estimating from my supervisor, because skill and good quotes win work. In year three I would buy my own test instruments and tools bit by bit, with no debt, and do small weekend jobs to build a name and a client list. In year four I would write a business plan with a cash flow forecast, register the business, get insurance and a TRN, and talk to a bank about a small loan for a used van. In year five I would leave my job with savings for at least three months of costs and a list of builders and clients ready to give me work. I would review the plan every six months.
markingPoints: Clear yearly milestones over five years
Licensing and qualifications early, with the reason
Builds experience, niche skills and pricing ability
Savings, equipment and legal set-up planned without heavy debt
First clients and contacts before leaving the job; regular review

essays.stem: Carry out a personal SWOT analysis for an electrician who wants to start a business specialising in solar PV and standby generator work, and explain how the results shape the strategy.
essays.modelAnswer: Strengths might be good technical skill, a Level 3 qualification, experience of solar installs with a past employer, and a good name with clients. Weaknesses might be little experience of pricing and running a business, no van, limited savings and weak record keeping. Opportunities include high electricity prices pushing homes and businesses towards solar, storms and outages raising demand for generators and changeover switches, and builders who need reliable subcontractors. Threats include larger solar firms with better prices, cheap unlicensed workers, changes in rules for connecting solar to the grid, and the cost of imported panels and batteries changing with the exchange rate. The strategy should use the strengths to grab the opportunities, for example by marketing tested, certified solar and generator work. It should fix weaknesses, by taking a short business course and saving for a van, and plan for threats, by keeping up with the rules and buying from more than one supplier.
markingPoints: Sensible strengths for this electrician
Sensible weaknesses
Opportunities linked to solar and generator demand in Jamaica
Threats such as competition, rule changes or import costs
Explains how the SWOT shapes the strategy (use strengths, fix weaknesses, plan for threats)

essays.stem: Explain how an electrical contractor should build up the price of a job, including materials, labour, overheads, profit, contingency and GCT. Use a small example.
essays.modelAnswer: First the contractor does a take-off from the drawings to list every material, and prices it from current supplier quotes, adding a small waste allowance. Next he estimates the hours for each task and multiplies by the charge-out rate, which already covers wages and overheads such as insurance, van, phone and tools. Some firms add overheads as a separate percentage instead. Then he adds a contingency for risks, such as hidden faults in an old building. Profit is added as a mark-up on the total cost. Finally, GCT is added at the current rate, shown as a separate line. For example, for a small shop: materials J$60 000, labour 20 hours at J$2 500 = J$50 000, total J$110 000. A 5% contingency adds J$5 500, making J$115 500. A 15% mark-up adds J$17 325, giving J$132 825 before GCT. The contractor should then compare with the market and check the price still gives a fair profit.
markingPoints: Materials from a take-off and current prices, with waste
Labour hours at a charge-out rate
Overheads included in the rate or as a percentage
Contingency and profit added
GCT added at the current rate as a separate line; correct worked example

essays.stem: Explain how to work out an hourly charge-out rate for a one-person electrical business, and why many new contractors set it too low.
essays.modelAnswer: The owner first decides the yearly wage he needs to live on. Then he adds up all the yearly overheads: van payments, fuel and repairs, insurance, licence fees, phone and data, tools and test instrument calibration, accounting, advertising and a share for replacing equipment. Next he works out the chargeable hours. A year may have about 2 000 working hours, but much time goes on travel, quoting, buying materials, paperwork and days with no work, so only perhaps 1 200 to 1 500 hours can be charged. The rate is the wage plus overheads, divided by the chargeable hours, and then profit is added. For example, J$2 000 000 wage plus J$1 000 000 overheads over 1 500 hours gives J$2 000 an hour before profit. Many new contractors set the rate too low because they compare it only with their old wage, forget overheads, count every hour of the year as chargeable, or try to undercut everyone, and then they cannot pay for their tools or van.
markingPoints: Starts from the wage needed
Adds all yearly overheads with examples
Uses realistic chargeable hours, not all working hours
Rate = (wage + overheads) ÷ chargeable hours, then profit; example
Explains why rates are set too low

essays.stem: Explain why a profitable electrical contractor can still run out of cash, and describe five ways to manage cash flow on large jobs.
essays.modelAnswer: Profit is worked out when the work is done and invoiced, but cash only arrives when the client pays. On a large job the contractor must pay for cable, boards and fittings, and pay wages every week, long before the client pays, so even a profitable job can leave the bank account empty. Late payers, retentions held back and buying too much stock make it worse. To manage cash flow, first, take a deposit before starting, enough to cover the first materials. Second, agree stage payments in the contract, tied to clear stages such as first fix, second fix and testing. Third, buy materials in stages as needed and agree credit terms with suppliers, so the firm pays them after the client pays. Fourth, invoice promptly and accurately, and follow up late payments politely but firmly. Fifth, keep a cash flow forecast up to date so shortfalls are seen early, with an agreed overdraft or savings as a buffer.
markingPoints: Explains the gap between profit and cash (paying out before being paid)
Deposit and stage payments
Buying in stages and supplier credit terms
Prompt invoicing and chasing late payers
Cash flow forecast and a buffer

essays.stem: Describe the legal, licensing, tax and insurance steps needed to set up and run an electrical contracting business in Jamaica, and why each matters.
essays.modelAnswer: The owner must hold the electrical licence the law requires for the work he will certify, because only licensed people may sign off installations for inspection and connection. The business name should be registered, or a company formed, so it is legal and the name is protected. The business needs its own TRN and must keep records for income tax, and it must register for GCT if its sales reach the level the tax authority sets, then charge and pay GCT at the current rate. When staff are hired, the owner must make payroll deductions, such as NIS, NHT, education tax and income tax, and pay them over on time. Insurance should include public liability, for harm or damage to others, employer's liability for staff, and cover for the van, tools and test instruments. A business bank account keeps business money separate. Each step keeps the firm legal, protects the owner and clients, and builds trust with builders, lenders and the public.
markingPoints: Electrical licence for certifying work
Business name registration or company, and a business bank account
TRN, income tax and GCT registration where required
Payroll duties when hiring staff
Insurance: public liability, employer's liability, vehicle and tools; says why each matters

essays.stem: Explain what a lender would expect to see in a business plan for a new electrical contracting firm, and how each section helps the lender decide.
essays.modelAnswer: A lender would expect a short summary of the business and the loan requested, so it can see quickly what is asked. It would want the owner's background, qualifications, licence and experience, to judge whether he can do the work and run a firm. A market section would show who the customers are, such as homeowners, builders and businesses, the competition and the demand, for example for solar and generator work, to show there is enough work. An operations section would describe the services, equipment, suppliers, premises and staff plans. A marketing section would show how clients will be found and how prices are set. The financial section matters most: start-up costs, the loan and how it is used, the owner's own money put in, a sales forecast, a cash flow forecast for at least twelve months, the break-even point and a projected profit and loss. A risk section would show the owner's plans for slow payment, competition or illness. Together these show whether the loan can be repaid.
markingPoints: Summary, and owner's skills, licence and experience
Market: customers, competition and demand
Operations and marketing plans
Financials: start-up costs, own money, cash flow forecast, break-even, profit forecast
Risks and how they are managed; links each to the lender's decision

essays.stem: Describe a marketing strategy for a new electrical firm in Mandeville that wants work from homeowners, builders and small businesses.
essays.modelAnswer: First the firm should be clear about what makes it different, for example licensed, tested and certified work, on-time arrival, clean sites and same-day emergency call-outs, and use this in all its messages. For homeowners, a simple social media page with photos of neat work, reviews and quick replies to messages works well, along with signs on the van and flyers at hardware stores. Word of mouth matters most, so every client should be asked to recommend the firm and leave a review. For builders, the owner should visit sites and building suppliers, meet contractors and architects, and give fast, clear quotations; doing the first jobs well and on time leads to repeat work. For small businesses, the firm could offer maintenance contracts, such as yearly testing and emergency cover, which give steady income. The firm should track where each enquiry came from, so it spends more on what works, and keep its prices fair rather than always the cheapest.
markingPoints: States a clear selling point
Methods for homeowners (social media, reviews, van signs, stores)
Methods for builders (networking, quick quotations, reliable first jobs)
Methods for small businesses (maintenance contracts)
Tracks results and avoids competing on price alone

essays.stem: Identify the main risks for a new electrical contracting business and explain how the owner can reduce each one.
essays.modelAnswer: One risk is not being paid, or paid late, which can sink a small firm. The owner reduces it with written contracts, deposits, stage payments and checking new clients. Another is pricing too low and losing money; careful take-offs, a proper charge-out rate and a contingency help. A third is an accident or electrical fault that injures someone or damages property. The owner reduces this through safe isolation, testing and inspection, trained staff, and public liability insurance. A fourth is the owner falling ill or being injured, since a one-person firm then earns nothing; savings, insurance and a trusted partner or subcontractor help. A fifth is theft of tools and the van, reduced by locking up, marking tools and insurance. Others include changing material prices, which short quote validity and supplier quotes help with, and too few jobs in a slow period, which a spread of clients and maintenance contracts helps with. The owner should list the risks, rate them and review them often.
markingPoints: Late or non-payment, with controls
Under-pricing, with controls
Accidents and faults, with safety and insurance controls
Owner illness, theft or price changes, with controls
Says risks should be listed, rated and reviewed

essays.stem: Explain how an electrical contractor should decide when and how to grow the business by hiring staff, and the new duties that come with being an employer.
essays.modelAnswer: The owner should look at the records first: is there steady work, with jobs turned away or delayed, and enough cash flow to pay a wage every week even in a slow month? A forecast should show that the extra work will more than cover the new wage, payroll costs and tools. Growth can start with a part-time helper or an apprentice, or by subcontracting to a trusted electrician, before taking on full-time staff. The owner should write a clear job description, choose fairly, and check qualifications and references. As an employer, the owner must give a written contract, pay at least the minimum wage, make payroll deductions such as NIS, NHT, education tax and income tax and pay them on time, and keep records. He must provide a safe workplace, training, PPE and supervision, and insurance for staff. He also becomes a leader, so he must plan the work, check quality and treat staff with respect, which takes time away from doing the work himself.
markingPoints: Uses records and forecasts to judge steady work and cash
Grows in steps (part-time, apprentice, subcontract)
Fair hiring: job description, checks
Employer duties: contract, wages, payroll deductions, records
Safety, training, PPE, insurance and leadership duties

practical1.title: Personal SWOT, niche choice and five-year strategy poster
practical1.brief: Each member writes a personal SWOT analysis for their own plan to run an electrical business. Then, as a team, research the local market for electrical work in your parish: each member gathers information from one source (an interview with a hardware or electrical store, a phone or role-played call with a builder or contractor, prices and services of three competitors found online or in person, or news on solar, generator or energy-saving demand). Together, choose one niche the team could serve, such as solar PV, standby generators, maintenance contracts or small commercial fit-outs, and give reasons. Produce a poster or chart with: the market findings, the chosen niche and its selling point, five SMART goals, and yearly milestones for five years (licence, experience, savings, equipment, first clients). Present the poster to the assessor, with every member presenting one part. Photograph each stage.
materials: Personal SWOT template for each member
Market research sheet and interview questions
Phone or computer with internet, if available
Chart paper, markers and sticky notes
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The market research sheets with notes from each source
The team choosing the niche, with the reasons written up
The finished poster with SMART goals and five-year milestones
checklist: Wrote an honest, specific personal SWOT
Gathered useful market information from their source and recorded it
Helped choose a niche with sound reasons
Wrote at least one goal that meets all the SMART points
Helped set realistic milestones for licence, savings, equipment and clients
Presented their part clearly and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Keep personal information in the SWOTs private within the group
Be polite and honest when contacting stores or contractors; say it is for a training task
Treat each other's ideas with respect
Keep bags and cables clear of walkways

practical2.title: Start-up budget, charge-out rate, break-even and cash flow forecast for a loan meeting
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a price list for a used van, tools, test instruments, PPE, insurance, licence and registration fees (all made up), a typical job mix and the GCT rate to use. As a team, plan a one-van electrical business for the niche of your choice. (1) Write a start-up budget and show how it is paid for (savings and a loan). (2) Work out the yearly overheads and the hourly charge-out rate, using a realistic number of chargeable hours. (3) Work out the break-even number of jobs a month. (4) Build a six-month cash flow forecast in a spreadsheet, with deposits, stage payments and loan repayments. (5) Price one sample job as a quotation, with GCT shown as a separate line. (6) Role-play a meeting with a loan officer (the assessor), presenting the figures. Each member prepares one of parts 1 to 5 and checks another member's figures, and every member speaks in the meeting. Photograph each stage.
materials: Price list, job mix and GCT rate (from the assessor)
Computers with a spreadsheet program, or calculators and forms
Budget, overheads, break-even and quotation forms
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The start-up budget with sources of money
The overheads list and charge-out rate working
The six-month cash flow forecast on screen
The sample quotation with GCT on a separate line
checklist: Prepared their part with correct figures and clear working
Included realistic overheads and chargeable hours
Showed deposits, stage payments and loan repayments in the cash flow
Priced the quotation correctly, with GCT shown separately at the given rate
Checked another member's figures and corrected any errors
Explained the figures clearly in the loan meeting
safety: This is a desk task: keep bags and cables off the floor and walkways
Sit with good posture and take short screen breaks
Keep the team's figures within the group
Be respectful in the role play
